On the readings, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan report that al-Hasan and Zayd ibn 'Ali read "rahmatun" in the nominative, implying "it is a mercy." No commentator draws a legal ruling from this verse; they confine themselves to explaining its meaning and construction.

This verse affirms that God is the Lord of the heavens, the earth and whatever lies between them, the Owner and Governor of all that is in them, and it calls on the polytheists, if they are truly certain of this, to recognise that there is no deity worthy of worship besides Him, since He gives life and causes death and is the Lord of the earliest and the latest generations. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and al-Sa'di agree that it presents an argument drawn from what the listeners already concede, their outward acknowledgment not being a sincere conviction, since they play and doubt. Al-Tabari judged both readings of "Lord of the heavens" acceptable, the nominative as a new predicate or resumption and the genitive as an apposition to "your Lord". Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi attach the genitive to the preceding phrase and the nominative to "He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing". Al-Zamakhshari, Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn Ashur explain the conditional clause as a challenge implying that their certainty is in fact lacking or incomplete. Al-Mawardi, al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud read "muqinin" as those who seek certainty, a minority reading. Ibn Ashur sees the verse as a return to addressing the polytheists, continuing the argument from creation. The commentators do not settle between these readings and present them as equally acceptable.

This verse states that there is no god but Allah, who gives life and causes death, and that He is the Lord of the addressees and of their earliest forefathers, and the commentators draw from these attributes the proof of God's oneness. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di explain that the address is to the polytheists, after God has established His lordship over the heavens and the earth, and that the condition "if you are certain" means that they should believe with certainty in what they are told, namely the Messenger and the Quran. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi observe that the condition implies their acknowledgement of divine lordship should rest on knowledge. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi note that the Kufan readers read "rabbi" in the genitive as an epithet, while the others read "rabbu" in the nominative, and al-Tabari holds both readings correct in meaning. Al-Qurtubi suggests that the certain person may be one who seeks certainty. On "but they are in doubt, playing", the commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri, take it to describe a profession of faith without certainty, based on imitating their fathers or on mockery. Al-Sha'rawi stresses that belief is a natural human disposition that surfaces in hardship. On these points the exegetes agree: the verse establishes monotheism and reproaches doubt and derision.

This verse states that the disbelievers, although they acknowledge that God is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, did not hold this acknowledgement with firm certainty, but were in doubt and playing. Commentators link the verse to what precedes it, namely the greatness of the Quran and its revelation on a blessed night: God is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, there is no god but Him, He gives life and causes death, and He is the Lord of your forefathers. If you are certain of this, the verse says, then the truth is in what the Messenger brings, but they were not certain. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Ashur agree that their acknowledgement did not come from true knowledge and was mixed with play, mockery or doubt. Al-Tabari adds that doubt so overwhelms them that it seems to surround them. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that the phrase 'if you are certain' means seeking certainty or an acknowledgement based on knowledge. Al-Qurtubi adds that their belief was only an imitation of their fathers, without knowledge. Commentators differ on the meaning of 'playing': most understand it as mockery of the Prophet and the Quran. Beyond the verse, opinions differ on the smoke mentioned in the surah. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and others identify it with the famine that struck the Quraysh when the Prophet invoked against them with years like the years of Joseph, while others regard it as a sign of the Hour. Ibn Kathir and al-Shawkani reconcile the two views. Some reports praise the surah, but scholars judged them weak.

In this verse God tells His Prophet ﷺ to wait for the day when the sky brings a clear smoke that covers the people, and it will be said to them that this is a painful punishment; they will then ask God to lift it and promise to believe. The commentators agree that the word ertaqib means to wait, and that the smoke is something to be feared. The meaning of the smoke, however, is disputed. Ibn Mas'ud, followed by Mujahid, Abu al-'Aliya, al-Nakha'i, al-Dahhak and al-Tabari, takes it to be the famine that struck Quraysh after the Prophet ﷺ prayed against them for years like the years of Joseph, so that a man saw between himself and the sky something like smoke from hunger; on this view the smoke has already passed, and the great seizure is the battle of Badr. Others, including Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, al-Hasan and Zayd ibn Ali, hold that it is one of the signs of the Hour, not yet come, which will enter the ears of the disbelievers and afflict believers like a cold. Ibn Kathir considers the view that it is a sign of the End more consistent with the general wording, while al-Razi finds Ibn Mas'ud's reading less fitting to the expressions used. A third opinion, reported by al-Mawardi and others, places the smoke on the day of the conquest of Mecca, when dust veiled the sky; Ibn Kathir regards it as very weak. Several commentators hold that both meanings may apply, and the reading tied to Quraysh is preferred by many.

God tells His Prophet to await the day when the sky brings a plain smoke that covers the people, and it will be said: this is a painful punishment. The disbelievers will then beg for the removal of the punishment, promising to believe. Commentators differ on this smoke. Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, Abu al-'Aliya, al-Dahhak and al-Tabari, with al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, take it to be the famine that struck Quraysh after the Prophet invoked against them years like the years of Joseph, so that a man saw something like smoke between himself and the sky from hunger. God lifted the affliction, but they returned to disbelief, and the great seizure is the Battle of Badr. By contrast, Ali, Ibn 'Abbas in one report, Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan and Abu Hurayra held that the smoke is one of the signs of the Hour which has not yet come: it enters the ears of the disbelievers and affects believers like a cold. Ibn Kathir prefers this second view, al-Razi judges the first closer to the context addressed to Quraysh, and Ibn 'Ashur reads the smoke as dust from dry ground. As for the great seizure, most commentators link it to Badr, while al-Hasan and 'Ikrima refer it to the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari also notes that several reports on this matter are disputed as to their soundness.

This passage has God tell His Prophet ﷺ to wait for the day when the sky brings a plain smoke that covers the people, and then the disbelievers will say: 'Our Lord, remove the punishment from us, and we shall believe.' The commentators agree that this is a conditional promise of faith made by the speakers should the affliction be lifted. They differ on what the smoke is. Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, Abu al-'Aliya, al-Dahhak and al-Nakha'i, followed by al-Tabari, identify it with the famine that struck Quraysh after the Prophet prayed against them for years like the years of Joseph, so that a person looking at the sky saw something like smoke from hunger; in their view this has already passed. Ibn 'Abbas in one transmission, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan and Zayd ibn 'Ali hold instead that it is one of the signs before the Hour, not yet come; Ibn Kathir follows this view while noting the famine reading. On the 'great seizure', most scholars, including Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid and Ubayy ibn Ka'b, identify it with the Battle of Badr, while al-Hasan, 'Ikrima and Qatada, and Ibn 'Abbas in another report, take it to be the Day of Resurrection. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir lean toward the latter, while al-Zamakhshari finds the famine reading closer to the text. Ibn 'Ashur adds that lifting the affliction may mean preventing an expected harm rather than removing one already present, and notes that the reports do not record any Qurayshi promise to convert.

God asks how the disbelievers could benefit from a reminder after the affliction has struck them, when a clear messenger has already come to them. Ibn 'Abbas reads the verse as meaning "how could they", and Mujahid as "after this calamity has befallen them". Al-Tabari sees it as a rejection of their repentance, since they turned away from the reminder when the messenger came. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi add that the signs and miracles already brought, above all the inimitable Book, were more fitting to prompt reflection than the lifting of the smoke. On the charge that he was "taught", al-Baghawi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan report that they said a human being taught him, while al-Razi also cites the view that jinn whispered to him, and Ibn 'Ashur reads the two accusations as made by different groups or at different times. As for the following verse, most commentators, including Ibn Mas'ud, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, understand that God will lift the punishment for a short while and they will return to disbelief; Qatada takes it as a return to the punishment of the Hereafter. The "greatest seizure" is the Battle of Badr according to Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid and others, while al-Hasan and Ikrima, and in one report Ibn 'Abbas, take it to be the Day of Judgement; al-Razi judges the latter view the sounder. These readings are not mutually exclusive, as Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud note.

This verse says that those who rejected the Prophet cannot be expected to take heed, for a clear messenger had come to them, yet they turned away and said he was taught or was mad. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read the opening question, how can they have remembrance, as a rejection of their promise to believe once the punishment is lifted. Al-Tabari adds that the messenger's clarity is meant to show them the truth of what is recited. The meaning of "taught" is discussed: al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud report that a non-Arab slave of a Thaqif man was said to be their teacher, while Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan note that the charge varied, some saying a human taught him and others naming soothsayers or devils. Al-Razi reports that some claimed jinn dictated to him during his fits of unconsciousness.

The next verse, saying that the punishment will be lifted for a little while and that they will return to disbelief, is read in two ways. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the punishment to be the famine that struck Quraysh, after which they went back to their old ways once it was lifted. Qatada reads it as a warning of a return to God's punishment in the Hereafter. Ibn Atiyya and al-Baqa'i take it as a means of establishing the proof against them and granting them respite.

Regarding "the greatest seizure", Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas and Mujahid say it refers to the Battle of Badr, while al-Hasan and Qatada say it is the Day of Resurrection. Al-Razi judges the latter view to be more sound, and Ibn Kathir considers the Day of Resurrection the apparent meaning, though he allows that Badr may also be meant.

The commentators explain that this verse announces that God will lift the punishment from the disbelievers for a short time, after which they will return to their disbelief and denial. They differ on the nature of the punishment. Ibn Mas'ud, Muqatil and most exegetes identify it as the famine that struck the Quraysh when the Prophet ﷺ invoked against them years like those of Joseph; God lifted it after he asked for rain on their behalf, and they went back to rejecting him. On this reading, the great seizing refers to the Battle of Badr. Qatada and Ibn Zayd identify the punishment with the smoke itself.

Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and others also report that the lifting may concern the smoke expected before the Day of Judgment, in which case the return to disbelief comes after it has passed. Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur read the verb as future: God will remove the punishment and then they will return, which happened after the Prophet's prayer. Al-Zamakhshari sees the removal as a brief pause before a quick relapse.

Most agree on the meaning of "returning" as going back to polytheism and disbelief. Some, such as al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi, allow that it may also mean returning to God's punishment or to the Fire if they do not believe. Ibn Kathir notes that this return does not imply they had believed before. Overall, the verse teaches that faith professed in distress does not last.

The commentators explain that the "great seizure" in this verse refers to God's vengeance on the disbelievers, but they differ on when it takes place. Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Abu al-'Aliya and, in one report, Ibn 'Abbas, understand it to be the Battle of Badr, when God struck the leaders of Quraysh with death and captivity after they returned to disbelief once the famine had lifted. This reading is adopted by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Abu Hayyan, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur, who see it as the full retribution in this world. Al-Hasan, 'Ikrima, Qatada and, in another report, Ibn 'Abbas, take it to be the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, a view al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Sam'ani judge the stronger, while al-Mawardi allows that it may be the Hour itself, the last of God's seizures. As for the smoke mentioned just before, one reading holds that it was the famine that struck Mecca after the Prophet ﷺ invoked a curse, so that people seemed to see a haze between heaven and earth; this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, Abu al-'Aliya, Muqatil and others. Others, including 'Ali, Ibn 'Umar, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and al-Hasan, regard it as a sign of the end of time that has not yet occurred. The most widely cited commentaries hold that the verse concerns the Quraysh and that the vengeance follows their return to disbelief.

This verse tells us that God tested the people of Pharaoh, the Copts, before the Quraysh by sending them Moses, a noble messenger. The commentators differ on what his nobility means. Al-Kalbi and Ibn Bahr take it to mean noble in the sight of God, Muqatil means good character, al-Farra' and Abu Sulayman mean high lineage among the leaders of his people, while al-Zamakhshari and those who follow him see an inherent nobility, since God sent no prophet except from the best of his people. The verses then spell out what Moses asked: that the servants of God, understood by Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd as the Children of Israel, be released, that they not exalt themselves against God, and that they accept the clear proof he brings. There is disagreement over the threat of stoning he fears. Ibn Abbas and Abu Salih take it as verbal abuse, while Qatada and al-Suddi take it as being stoned to death. Some read the phrase "servants of God" as a call to obedience, others as a demand for their freedom. The commentators agree on the story that follows: God commands Moses to leave by night with his people, to leave the sea calm until Pharaoh and his army enter it and drown, and that the gardens, springs, crops and dwellings they left behind passed to the Children of Israel. Some cite reports that the sky and earth wept for the believer, while others explain that the phrase only expresses contempt for a people whose good deeds never rose to heaven.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the story of Moses before Pharaoh and his people, and that it is cited both to console the Prophet ﷺ and to warn the Quraysh polytheists that earlier nations were tested by their messengers and were not spared punishment. According to most exegetes, "Adduu ilayya ibad Allah" means: release the Children of Israel and send them with me. Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Jawzi, among others, report another reading, in which it means that you should render to me obedience and faith in what I call you to. As for "Innee lakum rasoulun amin", it means that Moses is trustworthy regarding God's revelation and message, adding nothing to it and taking nothing from it, as Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur explain. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan hold that "an" here is explanatory, since the coming of a messenger implies a sense of speech, whereas others read it as a lightened form of the heavy particle. The exegetes agree that Moses was charged with freeing the Children of Israel from enslavement, and that his call to Pharaoh to believe followed from this mission. They also agree that the prohibition against exalting oneself over God means not to be arrogant toward His obedience or toward His messenger. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Abu Hayyan note a difference over what is to be rendered: some say it is the sending of the Children of Israel, others say it is obedience and faith.

This verse records what Moses told Pharaoh and his people: not to exalt themselves against God by disdaining His revelation and His messenger, and his promise to bring a clear proof of his mission. Most commentators understand "clear authority" as an evident proof or argument. Qatada speaks of a manifest excuse, while Yahya ibn Sallam describes a plain demonstration. As for "exaltation" (al-'uluw), al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari explain it as rebellion, arrogance and disobedience toward God, while al-Mawardi also records the reading that relates it to arrogance toward God's servants.

The commentators agree that Moses sought refuge with his Lord against being stoned. They differ on the meaning of "rajm". Ibn Abbas and Abu Salih take it as verbal abuse, such as calling him a sorcerer or a soothsayer, whereas Qatada, followed by Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya, understands it as stoning, Ibn 'Atiyya judging this the more apparent sense. Al-Suddi takes it as killing. Al-Tabari concludes that the word covers any harm inflicted on the one stoned, whether by speech or by hand.

Finally, the phrase "then leave me alone" is understood by most as a request to be left in peace and free from harassment. Ibn Kathir links it to a truce until God judges between them, while al-Razi stresses keeping apart, being neither with him nor against him.

This verse records Moses' words to Pharaoh and his people: he seeks refuge with God, his Lord and theirs, from their stoning him, that is, from being killed or harmed. The commentators differ on the meaning of stoning. Qatada, al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir take it as pelting with stones that leads to death, while al-Tabari also holds that stoning can be verbal or physical and so covers any harm. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Salih understand it as verbal abuse, such as calling Moses a sorcerer or a madman. Al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Sa'di read it as a threat to kill him, which is what the preceding verses describe. Al-Sam'ani and Ibn 'Atiyya find the killing reading more likely, since the people could reach him only through insult, not by killing. The following phrase, 'if you do not believe in me, then leave me alone', is read by most as a request to be left in peace. Differences over assimilating the final letter of the verb 'udtu' are recitational and do not change the meaning.

This verse records that Moses, after delivering his message to Pharaoh and his people, asked them to hand over the Children of Israel and not to exalt themselves against God by disobeying Him, and told them that he brought a clear proof. When they threatened to stone him, he sought refuge with God, his Lord and theirs. He then said that if they did not believe him, they should leave him alone and stop harming him. The commentators agree on the basic sense: he is asking to be left in peace. They differ on the meaning of stoning. Qatada, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as stoning to death, while Ibn Abbas and Abu Salih take it as verbal abuse, such as calling him a sorcerer. Al-Tabari prefers a broader reading in which Moses seeks protection from any harm, whether spoken or physical. Al-Baghawi and al-Sam'ani explain that the call to withdraw means leaving him neither with them nor against him. On the phrase not to exalt oneself against God, Ibn Abbas takes it as forbidding invented lies about God, Qatada as forbidding rebellion, Ibn Jurayj as forbidding self-magnification, and Yahya ibn Salam as forbidding arrogance. All agree that the clear proof is the evident argument supporting his mission.

The commentators explain that Moses, after Pharaoh and his people had called him a liar, refused to release the Children of Israel and threatened him with stoning, prayed to his Lord that these people were criminals, meaning idolaters and disbelievers. Most agree that the fa in fa-da'a implies an omitted clause such as that they persisted in rejection and harm, and that anna is a clause whose particle is understood, so the prayer is a complaint and a plea, as Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di put it. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baghawi and others note that the reading with a kasra implies an omitted verb of speech, and some report that his prayer was, "O God, hasten for them what they deserve for their crimes", while others cite his words, "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people".

God then commanded him to travel by night with his servants. On the meaning of rahw, which he was to leave as it is, the commentators differ: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ikrima take it as calm or dry, al-Dahhak as smooth and soft, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd as easy, and Ka'b as a path. Al-Tabari, whom Ibn 'Atiyya's linguistic note supports, prefers the sense of leaving the sea still in the state it was in, and Ibn Kathir reports that Moses wished to close it over the pursuers but was told to leave it.

On the blessings the people left behind, the exegetes list the gardens, springs, crops and the noble station, which some understand as platforms or assemblies and others as fine dwellings. On "the heaven and the earth did not weep for them", Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ali say that a believer has a gate in heaven for his deeds and a place of prayer on earth which weep for him, and that Pharaoh's people had neither, while al-Hasan takes it to mean the people of heaven and earth. Ibn Qutayba and others read it as hyperbole that magnifies the disaster.

This verse records God's command to Moses to take His servants, the believing Children of Israel, away by night, warning him that Pharaoh and his people would pursue them. The commentators explain that the "fa" in "fa-asri" links the command to Moses' prayer against his people, and that an unstated element, clear from the context, is understood. All agree that the "servants" are the Children of Israel and that travelling by night means leaving before dawn. The word "mutba'un" means that Pharaoh and his army would catch up with them. Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read the form "fa-isri" from "sara", while the other readers pronounce "fa-asri" from "asra", two equivalent forms. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the order came after the crossing of the sea, while others treat it as directly continuing the preceding speech. Ibn Kathir notes that the departure took place without asking Pharaoh's permission. According to Ibn 'Ashur, specifying the night confirms the literal sense of the journey and gives enough time to reach the shore before Pharaoh arrives. The commentators do not differ on the essential meaning, only on the wording and details.

After Moses leaves by night with the Israelites, God tells him to leave the sea as it is once he has crossed it, calm and open, because Pharaoh and his army are about to enter it and drown. The commentators largely agree that rahw means calm and stillness: al-Tabari cites a line of poetry describing camels walking slowly, and al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi follow this reading. Ibn 'Abbas, quoted by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, says the sea must be left as it is, without being struck again with the staff. Qatada, Ibn Kathir, Mujahid and 'Ikrima understand that it should remain a dry path, while al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak take it as smooth and easy ground, and al-Kalbi, al-Akhfash and Qutrub as a steady state. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that Moses wanted to close the sea by striking it, fearing pursuit, and was told not to. Al-Mawardi reports that Muqatil identifies the sea with the Nile, and al-Dahhak places the drowning at al-Qulzum. The verses that follow, listing the gardens, springs, crops and noble station left behind, prompt differences: al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi take the noble station to mean platforms or dwellings, and Ibn Kathir describes pleasant homes. On the verse saying that heaven and earth did not weep for them, the commentators agree that these people had no righteous deeds rising to heaven nor places of worship on earth, following a report transmitted from 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas.

This verse describes what Pharaoh and his people left behind after they were drowned: many gardens, flowing springs, crops, a noble dwelling place, and the luxury they had enjoyed. The commentators agree on the general meaning that all this comfort vanished. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya take the "other people" who inherited it to be the Children of Israel, though Ibn Atiyya notes that no histories report them ruling Egypt, while al-Hasan says they returned there after Pharaoh died. On the "noble station", Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr understand pulpits, Qatada fine places of gatherings and homes, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi speak of noble assemblies and dwellings. On "grace", Ibn Umar understands the Nile, Ibn Ziyad the land of Egypt for its abundance, and others the ease of life. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain "fakihin" as enjoying comfort and luxury, al-Sudi as rejoicing, and Ibn Atiyya as people who made light of gratitude for these blessings. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and others report that the sky and the earth did not weep for them, because they had left neither righteous deeds rising to heaven nor places of worship on earth, whereas a believer is mourned by the places where he prayed and the gates through which his deeds ascended.

The commentators explain that the phrase "and crops and a noble station" is part of a list of what Pharaoh and his people left behind after they were drowned: gardens, springs, fields and fine dwellings. On the meaning of "noble station", two main views emerge. Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan, followed by Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, take it to mean the pulpits or the seats of rulers, while Qatada, Abu 'Amr, al-Suddi and al-Biqa'i read it as fine residences or pleasant assemblies. Al-Tabari stresses the sense of beauty and splendour, and Ibn al-Jawzi lists several glosses including high rank. Readers differ on the vowel of the word maqam: most read it with a fatha, meaning the place of standing, while Qatada and others read it with a damma, meaning the place of dwelling. There is broad agreement that these possessions passed out of the hands of their owners, and most commentators, including al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, identify the heirs as the Children of Israel. Ibn 'Atiyya considers this view weak because there is no historical report of their return to Egypt, while al-Hasan is cited as saying they did return after Pharaoh's fall.

This verse describes what Pharaoh and his people left behind after they were drowned: many gardens, springs, fields, a noble dwelling and the comfortable, luxurious life they had enjoyed. The commentators agree on the general sense of lost wealth and ease. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that "a noble station" means a dignified place or seat, while Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abbas understood it as the pulpits or the thrones of kings. Qatada took it to mean something beautiful and pleasing. As for "comfort", Ibn Umar understood it as the Nile of Egypt, Ibn Ziyad as the land of Egypt for its abundance, and others as the general ease and prosperity they enjoyed. Most readers, followed by al-Tabari, read "fakihin" as "living in luxury", while Abu Ra'ja and al-Hasan read "fakihin" in a sense closer to joyful pride. Regarding the "other people" who inherited these things, Qatada and al-Hasan identify them as the Children of Israel, whereas Ibn Atiyya considers this view weak and thinks of people who ruled Egypt after the Copts. Finally, the phrase "the heaven and the earth did not weep for them" is explained by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ali as the absence of righteous deeds rising to heaven or of places of worship on earth, while al-Hasan, al-Razi and Ibn Qutayba read it as a figure of speech expressing their insignificance.

The commentators explain that this verse closes the account of the destruction of Pharaoh and his people: thus it was, the gardens, springs, crops, noble dwelling and comfort they enjoyed were taken from them, and these things were given as an inheritance to another people. Most exegetes identify these others as the Children of Israel, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi state, relying on the parallel verse in Surat al-Shu'ara: 'and We made the Children of Israel inherit it'. Qatada, followed by al-Hasan, holds that the Children of Israel returned to Egypt after Pharaoh's death and took possession of it. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy reject this view, since the histories do not record such a return, and Ibn Juzayy suggests that inheritance may simply mean being empowered to use the land. Others, such as al-Shinqiti and Ibn 'Ashur, hold that the heirs were non-Israelite peoples who ruled Egypt after the Copts; Ibn 'Ashur adds that the verse in al-Shu'ara speaks of goods taken from Egypt being given to the Children of Israel in Palestine, a striking comparison. As for 'thus', the commentators take it either as a comparison with the earlier expulsion or as an emphasis that the matter is just so. The overall purpose is a warning to the Meccan deniers drawn from the fate of those who came before them.

This verse says that the heavens and the earth did not weep for Pharaoh and his people, who were drowned in the sea, and that they were not given respite; their punishment was hastened. The commentators explain the word "weep" in several ways. Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn Abbas, with 'Ata', say that when a believer dies, the place where he prayed on earth and the channel by which his deeds ascended to heaven weep for him; Pharaoh's people had neither, so no one wept for them. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report narrations to this effect, and both note that the chain of the hadith of Anas cited on this point is weak, as al-Tirmidhi also said. 'Ata' and al-Suddi understood the heaven's weeping as the reddening of its edges, and al-Suddi linked this to the killing of Husayn ibn Ali. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi observe that the Arabs used this phrase for a great person's death to magnify the loss; here the sense would be to belittle these people, whose destruction changed nothing. Al-Hasan takes "the heaven and the earth" to mean their inhabitants: the angels and believers did not grieve but rejoiced. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi hold that a literal weeping is possible. The commentators do not decide between these readings.

This verse recalls God's favour upon the Children of Israel, whom He rescued from the humiliating torment inflicted by Pharaoh and his people, namely the killing of their sons, the enslavement of their women and the exhausting labour that degraded them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud all take this to be the meaning. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that the phrase 'from Pharaoh' may be an apposition making Pharaoh himself the torment, so severe were his abuses, or it may mean the torment coming from Pharaoh. Most commentators understand 'high' as arrogance and tyranny, while Ibn 'Atiyya takes it as an excessive elevation in transgression. Some readers, cited by al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan, read 'Man Fir'awn' as a question to stress the horror of the situation. Several exegetes connect the verse to the drowning of Pharaoh's army mentioned just before, seeing it as part of the story of Moses. As for the phrase 'chosen with knowledge over the worlds', the majority understand it as the choice of the Israelites over the peoples of their own time, whereas al-Razi and Abu Hayyan discuss a broader sense of preference. The verse ends by noting that God gave them signs that constituted a clear trial.

This verse recalls that God rescued the Children of Israel from the humiliating torment inflicted by Pharaoh, who slaughtered their sons, spared their women and subjected them to harsh labour, and that Pharaoh was a proud tyrant who was excessive in his transgression. The commentators agree that "from Pharaoh" is an apposition clarifying "the humiliating torment". They also agree that "elevated" refers to arrogance and domination over God and His servants. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain it this way, whereas al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan read it as a high rank among the excessive ones, taking "among the wasteful" as a second predicate or a circumstance. Al-Qurtubi notes that this height is not praise but excess, namely raising himself above the worship of God. The reading attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, "Who is Pharaoh?", reported by al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan, serves to emphasise the magnitude of his tyranny or to diminish him by leaving him unnamed. The commentators connect this passage to the drowning of Pharaoh and his army, presented as a favour granted to the Children of Israel. Ibn 'Ashur also sees here an allusion to God's protection of believers in Mecca against the polytheists.

In this verse God says that He chose the Children of Israel with knowledge of their condition and preferred them over the people of their time. Most commentators, such as Qatada and Mujahid, explain that "the worlds" means the peoples of their era rather than all creation, and some support this by citing the verse calling the Muslim nation the best community raised up for mankind. All agree that "with knowledge" means that God knew they deserved this choice, though some, like Abu Hayyan, add that He knew they would sometimes go astray. Al-Tabari, Qatada and Mujahid take the choice to be a preference over their contemporaries, while al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir connect it to prophethood, mission and faith, and Ibn al-Jawzi links it to their deliverance from Pharaoh. The commentators also differ on the next verse: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the trial to be a clear blessing or a test, while Ibn Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari stress a manifest favour or a plain test that shows how people act, citing signs such as the parting of the sea, the shading cloud, and the manna and quails. Several commentators relate reports that the sky and earth wept over the believer and over al-Husayn, which Ibn Kathir considers weak, preferring to understand the weeping as the halting of good deeds rising to heaven and the loss of a believer's place of prayer on earth.

The commentators explain that this verse refers to the Children of Israel, to whom God gave signs that were a clear trial for them. They differ on what this trial consists of. Qatada, al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud take it to be a manifest favour, citing the parting of the sea, the shading cloud, and the sending down of manna and quails. Ibn Zayd understood it as a testing through both ease and hardship, citing the verse "We test you with evil and with good". Al-Farra' took it to mean a severe punishment.

Al-Tabari concludes that both meanings should be accepted together, since no evidence favours one over the other and God did test them in both ways. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the signs may also refer to Moses' miracles, such as the staff and the white hand, according to al-Farra'. Al-Razi adds that God tests through blessings as well as through trials, so that the sincere is distinguished from the hypocrite. Several scholars, including al-Shawkani, al-Alusi and al-Qasimi, see these signs both as proof given to the Children of Israel and as a test of their gratitude or ingratitude.

This passage reports the claim of the Quraysh disbelievers who denied the resurrection: they say that there is only this first death they undergo in the world, with no life or resurrection after it. The commentators explain that their demand, "bring us our fathers," was a challenge to revive their dead ancestors as proof that resurrection is true. Most of them agree that "these people" are the idolaters of Makkah, and that the demonstrative term belittles them. On the meaning of "our first death," al-Zamakhshari understands it as a death followed by life, while al-Razi holds that it means nothing will come to them after death. Ibn 'Ashur reads the phrase as a denial of any further life. The next verse recalls the destruction of earlier peoples, including the people of Tubba', and the commentators stress that their guilt was the cause of their ruin. About Tubba' himself opinions differ: some, such as Ibn Kathir, relate that he was a righteous man who embraced faith, while others consider the reports about him weak, and several decline to decide between the views.

This passage reports the claim of the Quraysh that denied resurrection: after this one death we suffer in this world, there is no other life, and we will not be raised. Commentators explain the phrase "the first death" in different ways. Al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir take it to mean that there is no second death after this one. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan understand that they meant the only death that is followed by a life, so their words amount to saying there is only our life in this world. Al-Razi adds that no other state will come upon them after this death. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the word "first" simply refers to the earlier death, without intending a contrast.

The commentators agree that the verse rejects resurrection. Their demand "bring us our fathers" is a call to revive their dead as proof of the Prophet's truthfulness. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that they asked for Qusayy ibn Kilab to be raised so they could question him, while al-Zamakhshari links the address to the believers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that the address is to the Prophet alone, out of respect, as al-Farra reports, whereas al-Qurtubi also mentions an address to him and his followers. Several, including al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi, answer that resurrection serves recompense in the hereafter, not testing in this world.

The verse then turns to Tubba' and his people, whose story is reported in varied ways. Qatada describes him as a Himyarite king, and Ibn Kathir notes that 'A'isha and Ka'b considered him righteous, since God blamed his people without blaming him. Traditions forbidding insult to him are judged weak by some. The general meaning is that the Quraysh are no better than these peoples, and that crime is what brings destruction.

The verse reports the words of the Meccan unbelievers who deny resurrection: for them there is only this first death in the world, with no life or raising afterward. They then challenge the Prophet ﷺ and those who believe him: bring back our fathers who have died, if you are truthful that God will raise them alive. The commentators agree that the address is to the Prophet and to the believers who promised resurrection, and that the purpose is to mock and to demand a sign that would confirm the promise. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the address is to the Prophet alone, using the plural as in the verse 'my Lord, send me back', while al-Farra' and Abu Hayyan take it as addressed to him and his followers. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi relate that Abu Jahl asked that Qusayy ibn Kilab be raised, since he was reputed truthful and could be questioned about the afterlife; al-Mawardi calls this an extremely weak objection, because the restoration is for recompense, not for accountability. Ibn Kathir calls the argument false, since the resurrection will come on the Day of Judgment and not in this world. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain the phrase 'our first death' as a denial that any state follows the first death, since they had been told of a death followed by life. Ibn Juzayy and Abu al-Su'ud describe it as a challenge meant to show the Prophet's inability. The following verse about the people of Tubba' receives extended treatment: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi identify him as a Himyarite king, while Aisha and Ka'b call him a righteous man, and Ibn Kathir reports a version in which he converted. Al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan note that the hadiths on him are weak and that the name may refer to several kings of Yemen. The general meaning is a warning that the earlier peoples were destroyed for their crimes.

God puts a rhetorical question of reproach to the Quraysh: are they better than the people of Tubba' and those before them whom He destroyed? According to the commentators, the meaning is that they are no better than those peoples in strength, power, wealth or standing, and that the reason for those peoples' destruction was their criminality, namely their disbelief and sins. If the Quraysh are equally guilty, they cannot expect to escape the same fate. The commentators agree that the verse is a warning addressed to the Quraysh. As for Tubba', most scholars, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, identify him as a righteous king of Himyar, some saying he was a believer or had embraced Islam. They rely on the fact that God blamed his people without blaming him, on the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd, 'Do not curse Tubba', for he had embraced Islam', and on a statement of 'A'isha that he was a righteous man. Some hadith scholars have weakened the chain of this hadith, as Ibn Kathir and others note. Ibn 'Abbas holds that he was a prophet, while a narration attributed to the Prophet says, 'I do not know whether Tubba' was a prophet or not'. Others, such as al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan, argue that Tubba' was a title for any king of Yemen. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take the superiority to be in strength and power, not in religion. Most recount briefly how Tubba' marched on Medina intending to destroy it, then turned back after two Jewish rabbis advised him, and how he honoured the Ka'ba.

God states that He did not create the heavens, the earth, and what lies between them in play or in vain, but in truth, meaning with a wisdom that requires reward for good and punishment for evil. The commentators agree on this general sense: creation would have no purpose if there were no resurrection or judgment, so the verse answers those who deny resurrection. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi explain that play means heedlessness or vanity, and that a world without recompense would be a game. Al-Tabari adds that God created beings to test them through commands and prohibitions. Al-Razi sees the verse as a decisive proof of resurrection, and he notes that the Mu'tazilites used it to argue that God neither creates nor wills disbelief, an argument he considers already answered. Al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and al-Baghawi report that the truth may mean justice, recompense, or the affirmation of God's oneness, without choosing among these readings. Several exegetes observe that most people fail to grasp this wisdom, which explains their lack of fear or hope. On the reading of the word for appointed time, al-Zamakhshari records an unusual variant, and Abu Hayyan notes another reading of the pronoun. The commentators link the verse to the Day of Judgment, the day on which people will be separated from their kin and their helpers.

God states that He did not create the heavens, the earth and what lies between them in play or in vain, but in truth, meaning with the wisdom and seriousness without which the order of the cosmos could not be sustained. The commentators explain that the verse points to the truth of resurrection and recompense: creation is not left without trial or accountability, since people are tested through commands and prohibitions and each is repaid for their deeds. Al-Tabari explains that "most of them" refers to the polytheists who do not know that God created this for them, and who, denying the return, neither fear His wrath nor hope for His reward. Abu Hayyan and others take the disbelievers of Mecca to be meant. Al-Shawkani and al-Alusi understand "the truth" as justice and recompense. The commentators agree that creation is not futile and that denying resurrection stems from ignorance of this wisdom. Some link the verse to what follows: the Day of Judgement, when God gathers all creatures, when no relative benefits another, and when only those whom God shows mercy are helped. The exegetes do not choose between these readings, which they present as closely related meanings.

The commentators explain that the Day of Decision is the Day of Resurrection, so called because God judges between His creatures according to their deeds, rewarding the good for their good and punishing the wicked for their evil. All of humanity has its appointed time on that day. Most scholars, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di, understand that no close relative can benefit or help another against God's punishment, and that the exception refers to the believer whom God has mercy upon, whom prophets and angels may intercede for, as Ibn 'Abbas is cited by al-Razi. Al-Tabari prefers reading the word man as nominative, meaning that the one God shows mercy to will be aided through intercession. The grammarians disagree: al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' take it as a disjunctive exception in the accusative, while al-Zamakhshari reads it as an apposition. One reading puts miqatahum in the accusative as the subject of inna, making the Day of Decision its predicate. Ibn 'Ashur holds the exception to be connected and to include intercession, while others treat it as disconnected. Some, such as al-Razi, understand the day as the separation of truth from falsehood, others as the separation of a person from his kin. In context, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi link these verses to a warning to the Quraysh through the reminder of past peoples, including Tubba' of Himyar, whose status is debated.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the Day of Decision, when God separates all creatures and repays each for what they did. On that day no close relative can avail another, and no one can be helped against God's punishment. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy agree that neither kinship nor friendship will protect anyone then, and that the negation covers every kind of protector, including a cousin, a relative, a friend or a freed slave. Ibn 'Atiyya reports that the final pronoun, 'nor will they be helped', may refer to the disbelievers; the exception 'except those on whom God has mercy' is then discontinuous, meaning that whoever God shows mercy to needs no human aid. This view is attributed to al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', as cited by al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya. The majority, including al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi, take the exception to refer to believers, who intercede for one another with God's permission, so the exception is continuous. Al-Tabari prefers reading 'man' in the nominative case. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Abbas explain that the expected helper may be a relative in faith, in lineage or a freed slave, and that if these do not help, others certainly will not. Ibn 'Ashur adds that intercession is itself a form of help granted by God. The verse closes by describing God as mighty in His vengeance against His enemies and merciful toward His friends.

The commentators explain that this verse speaks of the Day of Decision, the Day of Resurrection on which God judges between creatures and repays each one for his deeds. On that day no close relative can benefit another and no one can be shielded from God's punishment by the help of others. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and others agree that the exception in "except those on whom God has mercy" refers to the believers, who may intercede for one another with God's permission. They add that God is the Mighty who takes vengeance on His enemies and the Merciful toward His allies. Al-Tabari considers this the most correct interpretation. On grammar the scholars differ: the grammarians of Basra take "man" as a substitute for the pronoun in "yunsarun" or as a subject whose predicate is implied, while al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' read it as a disjunctive exception, meaning that whoever God has shown mercy to needs no one. Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari set out these readings without choosing between them. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the exception is connected and links God's mercy to His pleasure with His servant. Several commentators note that the context concerns the disbelievers of Mecca who denied the resurrection, and that the verse follows the statement that creation was not without purpose.

This verse describes the zaqqum tree, which grows at the base of the Blazing Fire, and declares its fruit to be the food of the sinner. The commentators agree that the athim is the disbeliever or the one who piles up sins. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi mention that many identify him with Abu Jahl, while noting the meaning is wider than one man. Ibn Abbas is quoted saying that a single drop of this fruit, if sent down to the world, would ruin people's livelihoods, and the tree is generally described as bitter and repugnant food.

The word al-muhl is explained in different ways. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir relate it to the dregs of olive oil, whereas others, such as several reports from Ibn Mas'ud cited by al-Tabari, liken it to molten silver or copper. Al-Zamakhshari also takes it as molten silver and copper. This substance boils in the bellies like scalding water. The readings differ on the verb yaghli: the feminine form refers back to the tree, the masculine to the food. Al-Tabari holds that both readings are correct, while Abu Ubayd preferred the masculine.

The commentators then describe the punishment: the guardians are ordered to seize the sinner, drag him roughly into the middle of the Fire, and pour boiling water over his head. The words "Taste it, for you were the mighty, the noble" are, in most views, a mocking rebuke, which al-Razi and Ibn Kathir link to Abu Jahl's boasting. Al-Zamakhshari also notes the variant readings of the particle. The verse closes by reminding them that this is what they used to doubt.

The commentators explain that "the food of the sinner" refers to the tree of zaqqum, whose fruit is the food of the one who piles up sins, and for most of them the greatest sin is disbelief in God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi take the word in its general sense of a wicked person, while Ibn Juzayy, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi say it means the disbeliever as a class, not one individual. Several scholars, including Ibn Zayd, al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi, identify the sinner in this verse as Abu Jahl, a view reported by al-Baghawi and repeated in the Jalalayn.

The word al-muhl is explained by Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar as the dregs of olive oil, and by others as molten metal such as silver, copper or iron, as Abu Hayyan reports. Al-Tabari also cites a report that Ibn Mas'ud melted silver to show what al-muhl looks like. The verb "yaghli" is read in the feminine by most reciters to agree with the tree, while Ibn Kathir and Hafs read it in the masculine to agree with the food; al-Tabari considers both readings correct.

The commentators agree that "fa'tiluhu" means to drag or push the sinner roughly toward the middle of the Fire, as al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir explain. The phrase "dhuq" is almost unanimously read as a mocking address. Al-Qurtubi, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir relate the story of Abu Jahl boasting that he was the most honoured man of Quraysh. On the reading of the Qur'an, al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi note that Abu Hanifa allowed recitation in Persian under a condition, while his companions rejected this view.

This verse describes the zaqqum tree of Hell as the food of the sinner. The commentators explain that al-athim means the disbeliever and polytheist, and al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi note that some identify him as Abu Jahl, though the verse is broader. Regarding al-muhl, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar take it to be the dregs of olive oil, while al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari report that it is molten metal, silver, iron or lead. Ibn Mas'ud, cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya, melted silver before people to illustrate it. This food boils in the bellies like scalding water. The readings differ: most read the verb in the feminine, referring it to the tree, while Ibn Kathir and Hafs read it in the masculine, referring it to the food. Al-Tabari considers both readings sound. The angels are ordered to drag the sinner to the middle of the Fire and pour boiling water over his head. Al-Zamakhshari reads the pouring as a metaphor, while Ibn Kathir takes it literally with the bodily effects. He is told mockingly: taste it, for you are the mighty and the noble, which Qatada and Ibn Atiyya link to Abu Jahl's boasting. The verse ends by saying that this is what they used to doubt.

This verse describes the food of the people of the Fire: the fruit of the zaqqum tree is the food of the great sinner, which most commentators take to mean the disbeliever or polytheist, and some name Abu Jahl specifically. Al-Muhl is explained by Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar as the dregs of oil, while Ibn Mas'ud and, in another report, Ibn Abbas take it to be molten gold, silver, iron or lead. Al-Hamim is water heated to the peak of its boiling. The commentators agree that this food seethes in the bellies of the disbelievers like boiling water. The readings differ on the verb: most read taghli in the feminine, referring to the tree, while Ibn Kathir and Hafs read yaghli in the masculine, referring to the food. Al-Tabari holds that both readings are valid and have the same meaning. Several scholars, including al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, report that a single drop of zaqqum falling on earth would ruin the livelihood of its people, and some present this as a saying of the Prophet. The commentaries then describe the punishment: the angels seize the sinner and drag him to the middle of Hell, pour boiling water over his head, and say to him mockingly, Taste it, you who were mighty and noble. Zamakhshari and others explain this irony as a taunt aimed at one who boasted of his strength and honour among his people. All agree that this is the torment they used to doubt in this world.

This verse describes the command given to the guardians of Hell to seize the sinner, whom many commentators identify as Abu Jahl, and to drag him violently to the midst of the Blazing Fire. Nearly all exegetes agree on the basic sense of the verb 'utila: to push and pull with force. Al-Tabari, citing Mujahid, takes it as pushing, al-Hasan as dragging, and al-A'mash as breaking like dry wood. Most explain 'sawa' al-Jahim' as the centre of the Fire, as Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak say, while al-Hasan takes it to mean its greatest part. On the reading, al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi hold that both vowellings of the letter ta' are correct dialects. The commentators then explain that pouring boiling water over the head means a punishment that penetrates the body down to the belly, as al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir note. The words 'taste it, you are the mighty, the noble' are, according to Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan, mocking and rebuking: the sinner had thought himself powerful and honoured among his people. The commentaries thus agree on the severity of this punishment, and there are no notable disagreements on it.

This verse describes the punishment of the sinful disbeliever in the Fire. The commentators explain that the angels appointed over Hell are commanded to seize him, drag him violently to the middle of the blaze, and then pour over his head some of the torment of boiling water, the hamim. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy agree that the sinner is the disbeliever and that it is really the boiling water that is poured, but that the phrase "torment of the hamim" is more forceful and more terrifying. Several add, on the authority of reports transmitted from Muqatil, that the keeper strikes the head with an iron club, splits the skull, and pours in the scalding water, which tears through the body; Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite this account.

Regarding the verb "fa'tiluhu", the two readings, with the letter ta vowelled with a kasra or a damma, are both accepted by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Atiyya as correct forms with the same meaning: to push and drag with force. Ibn Qutayba and Ibn al-Jawzi relate it to leading someone by force toward a prison or an ordeal. Al-A'mash takes it to mean breaking, as dry wood is broken.

On "the middle of the Blaze", Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak say it means its centre, while al-Hasan says it means its most intense part. The words "taste it, for you are the mighty, the noble" are, in the view of most commentators, said ironically to Abu Jahl, who boasted of his power and nobility.

This verse is addressed to the sinner in Hell, the arrogant disbeliever who boasted of his power and nobility in this world. It is spoken as a mocking, reproachful rebuke: taste this punishment, for you used to claim that you were the mighty, the noble. Most commentators link the verse to Abu Jahl. Qatada, Muqatil and Ikrima report that he boasted that he was the mightiest and most honoured man between the two mountains of Mecca, and the verse answers him. Al-Tabari regards the words less as praise than as a quotation of his own claims, used to humiliate him: in truth he is the lowly and despised one. Ibn Abbas reads it as meaning that you are neither mighty nor noble. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muqatil take it as mockery, Qatada as meaning mighty in your own eyes, and al-Mawardi as mighty among your people and honoured by them.

The commentators agree that the words are addressed to those who denied the resurrection, reminding them that this punishment is what they doubted in life. Al-Tabari links the word imtira' to doubt and dispute. In recitation, most readers use the kasra on "inna", beginning a new sentence, while al-Kisa'i reads the fatha on "anna", meaning "because". Al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan note that the intended meaning is the same although the grammatical analysis differs. Ibn al-Qayyim observes that the context clearly points to humiliation.

Ibn Kathir and others dwell on the scene of the guards of Hell, and Ibn Kathir notes that the report of the Prophet's encounter with Abu Jahl is transmitted in a mursal form. Al-Jaza'iri stresses that mockery and humiliation form a particularly painful punishment of their own.

This verse, part of the description of the punishment of the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, reports what will be said to the damned as a rebuke and mockery: this is the torment you used to doubt. The commentators explain that the verb tamtarun means to doubt and dispute. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya, the words 'Taste it, for you were the mighty, the noble' are said ironically, meaning in fact that you are humiliated and debased. Many exegetes connect the preceding verses to Abu Jahl, who boasted that he was the mightiest and noblest between the two mountains of Mecca. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the reading with kasra on the inna is that of the majority of readers, while al-Kisa'i read it with fatha; Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Tabari prefer the kasra, while others consider that both readings give the same meaning. The commentators explain that al-Muhl is the sediment of oil or molten metal, and al-Hamim is extremely hot water. The phrase fa'tilûhu means to drag and push him with violence into the middle of Hell. For some, such as Ibn Juzayy, the poured substance is in fact the torment itself, used figuratively. The verse therefore affirms that the disbelievers are reminded of what they denied.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the reward of the God-fearing, following the description of the punishment of the disbelievers earlier in the surah. They will be in a secure dwelling, where they no longer fear what troubled them in this world: sorrows, afflictions and Satan, and where they are safe from death and from being expelled. Many commentators agree that this secure place is Paradise itself. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy explain that calling the place "secure" is a metaphor, as a frightening place seems to betray its occupant, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan take the sense to be a place in which people are kept safe.

Readers differ on the vowelling of the word "maqam". Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "muqam" with a damma, meaning a place of residence, while the others read "maqam" with a fatha, meaning a place of standing or an assembly. Al-Tabari considers both readings correct and equivalent in meaning. Al-Mawardi records three interpretations of the security: protection from Satan and sorrows according to Qatada, from punishment according to al-Kalbi, and from death according to Muqatil.

The rest of the commentary describes the blessings: gardens and springs, garments of sundus and istabraq, and seating face to face. Ibn Kathir sees this as a contrast with the tree of zaqqum and the boiling water mentioned earlier. The commentators agree that this blessing is a gift of God's grace rather than something earned by deeds, as Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir report. Al-Sa'di stresses the completeness of joy and tranquillity in this dwelling.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the abode of the pious in the Hereafter: a secure place where they are safe from Satan, from sorrow, from death and from punishment. This secure place is made up of gardens and springs, the verse being an apposition that specifies the "secure station" mentioned just before. Al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn Kathir state that the security covers fear of death, of being expelled, of every worry and fatigue, and of Satan, while al-Kalbi and Muqatil add that it means safety from punishment and from death. On the readings "maqam" and "muqam", al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari hold that both are close in meaning: the first refers to the place where one stands, the second to the place of dwelling. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan see in the description the combination of the conditions of a pleasant dwelling, with its gardens and springs. Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud note that the picture stands in contrast to the zaqqum tree and the boiling water mentioned just before. The commentators do not disagree on the meaning of gardens and springs; their differences concern mainly the scope of the notion of security and the comforts of life that follow from it.

This passage describes the reward of the righteous in Paradise. They dwell in a secure place, which the commentators identify with gardens and springs, where nothing threatens them with loss or harm. They wear silk garments: al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn Kathir explain that sundus is fine silk and istabraq thick silk, while al-Mawardi reports several views, including that sundus is what they wear and istabraq what they recline on. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that istabraq is a Persian loanword which, once Arabized, becomes part of the Arabic of the Quran. The word « mutaqabilin » is understood by most as meaning that they face one another and no one sees another's back, since their couches turn with them; al-Mawardi also cites the sense of mutual love without enmity. Several commentators report that the believers receive wives with large, beautiful eyes, which some, such as al-Hasan, understand as renewed creations rather than women of this world. On the exception « except the first death », most read it as meaning « other than », al-Tabari takes it as « after », and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya discuss its grammatical basis. The commentators agree that the believers are saved from the fire by God's grace and that no death will reach them in Paradise after the one they already experienced in this world.

The commentators explain that God, who honoured the righteous in Paradise with gardens, springs and silk garments, also honoured them by pairing them with the houris, women of dazzling fair complexion with large, beautiful eyes. Most agree that the word hur means women who are intensely white with dark eyes, and that ayn is the plural of ayna', a woman with large eyes. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi connect the word to the notion of intense whiteness, whereas Mujahid and Qatada understand it as the radiant beauty and clear complexion that make the gaze wander. Some rely on Ibn Mas'ud's reading bi-'ays 'in, meaning the white ones. On the question of marriage, Yunus and Abu 'Ubayda take the verb to mean joining in pairs rather than a marriage contract, since there is no legal obligation in Paradise, while others say the term allows both meanings. Regarding the phrase that they will not taste death there except the first death, most treat the exception as meaning 'other than' or 'after', so that they will never die again, the first death being the one already undergone in this world. Ibn Qutayba holds that the blessed see their places in Paradise before dying, making the exception a continuous one. All stress that this bounty is a grace from God and that piety is the cause of the great success.

This verse describes the righteous in Paradise asking for every kind of fruit they desire, feeling secure. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that this security means they fear neither the end nor the failure of these fruits, unlike the fruits of this world, which can be unavailable at certain times. Qatada, followed by several commentators, takes it to mean security from death, illness and Satan. Al-Qurtubi reports both explanations together, while al-Shawkani, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Qasimi widen the meaning to include any harm or displeasure.

The commentators agree on the general sense: the verb translated as asking here means requesting or ordering that what one desires be brought. Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari note that these fruits are tied to no particular place or time. Ibn Sa'di adds that some fruits have no name or equivalent in this world and come without effort. Al-Jalalayn specifies that the requests are addressed to the attendants.

The verse connects to the next, which states that no death will be tasted in Paradise after the first. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi read the exception as meaning "after", while al-Farra, al-Zajjaj and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as "other than". Ibn Qutayba explains that the blessed, at their death, already see their dwellings in Paradise.

This verse says that the righteous believers in Paradise will never taste death again, that the first death they suffered in this world is their last, and that God has spared them the torment of the Blazing Fire out of His grace. The commentators agree that the bliss and eternity of Paradise are a divine favour rather than something earned by deeds alone, and that this is the great triumph. They differ over the meaning of the exception 'except the first death'. Al-Tabari takes 'illa' to mean 'after', while al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutayba read it as a disjunctive exception, meaning 'but the first death they have already tasted'. Others read it as 'other than', and Ibn Qutayba makes it a connected exception, arguing that the blessed see their places in Paradise at the moment of death. Ibn al-Qayyim finds the 'after' reading very fine, and al-Qurtubi reports several of these readings. On the houris, Mujahid describes women whose gaze is dazzled by their beauty, while Qatada and Abu 'Ubayda take them to be fair-skinned women with wide eyes; al-Hasan holds that they are the aged women of this world made anew. Some explain that the verb 'married' here means 'paired with', not a marriage contract. All explain the fruits as every kind desired, and 'secure' as free from cessation, harm, sickness and death.

The commentators explain that this verse concludes the description of the reward of the righteous in Paradise: what they receive, and their protection from the punishment of the Blazing Fire, is a bounty from their Lord rather than a mere entitlement earned by their deeds. Al-Tabari holds that God spared them out of grace, and that without this pardon they would have suffered the pain they deserved; Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya agree, and al-Zamakhshari reads it as a gift and a reward from God. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi offer other meanings for the neighbouring verses. Al-Razi argues that reward is a grace and not a strict right, while the judge 'Abd al-Jabbar holds that most of what they receive is owed to their deeds, though it is ultimately a divine favour. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi cite the hadith of Abu Hurayra that no one enters Paradise by his deeds alone, and as-Sa'di cites the same hadith. On the particle 'illa' in 'except the first death', al-Tabari takes it to mean 'after', al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj to mean 'other than', al-Zamakhshari as an exclusion based on an impossible condition, and Ibn Qutayba holds that the righteous, having died in this world, are already joined to the causes of Paradise. Al-Razi offers several further readings, including that true Paradise is knowledge and love of God. The commentators note that the people of Paradise neither die nor grow old. As-Sa'di explains the great triumph as God's pleasure and safety from His punishment, while al-Jaza'iri explains it as deliverance from the Fire and entry into Paradise.

The commentators explain that this verse means God made the Qur'an easy to recite and understand in the Arabic language of the Prophet ﷺ, so that his people might reflect, take heed, and return to obedience to their Lord. The pronoun refers to the Qur'an. Most read "your tongue" as the Arabic language, while al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya relate it to recitation. Al-Mawardi gives two senses of "that they may remember": that they return to God, or that they learn a lesson.

The second part, "So wait, and they too are waiting," is read in several ways. Al-Tabari and Qatada take it as the Prophet awaiting victory, while the disbelievers await his defeat. Al-Mawardi, citing an-Naqqash, reports that they await his death. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya read a promise to the Prophet and a warning to his opponents. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that some consider the verse abrogated by the verse of the sword, a view he rejects. Al-Qurtubi also offers the reading that it refers to awaiting the Day of Judgment.

Al-Shawkani, al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur place the verse as a summary closing the surah. Ibn 'Ashur adds that it rebukes those who rejected the Qur'an despite its clarity in their own language, and that its ease of understanding is linked to the Arabic tongue.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to wait: the disbelievers are waiting for his defeat and downfall, while he awaits the victory God has promised him. The commentators agree that it contains both a promise to the Prophet and a warning to the deniers. As to what the waiting means, opinions differ. Qatada, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as waiting for the victory and conquest from God, while the polytheists await his defeat. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi say it may refer to waiting for the punishment that will strike the wrongdoers, and al-Naqqash reports that they await the Prophet's death. Al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan mention waiting for the Day of Judgment, the Day of Separation. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya see the verse as a call to leave the opponents alone, which they say was abrogated by the verse of the sword, though Ibn al-Jawzi disputes this abrogation. Several commentators note that the verse closes the surah by returning to its themes: the Qur'an was made easy in the Arabic tongue so that people might remember. Some commentaries cite hadiths on the merit of reciting the surah, but the exegetes do not rely on them to explain the meaning of the verse.
